coverage: Covering roughly Nov 27–28, 2026, from his X lists, home timeline and saved posts. Compiled Saturday morning, ET.

items.headline: Aschenbrenner's 167-page letter: AI labs could pass a $1 trillion run rate by end-2027
items.summary: Leopold Aschenbrenner's Situational Awareness LP published its Q3 letter, and it took over the investing timeline overnight. Its core claim, as quoted by @firesidealpha: Anthropic and OpenAI could together exit 2027 above $1 trillion in annualized revenue, with Anthropic alone "plausibly approaching $1T," and the market is pricing far slower AI progress than the fund expects. @FunOfInvesting called it a strong case for the compute thesis; @oguzerkan called it linear extrapolation written to persuade investors.
items.short: Situational Awareness's Q3 letter argues lab revenue could top $1 trillion a year by end-2027.

items.headline: Older chips, higher rent: the letter says compute owners now set the price
items.summary: The detail @ren_stocks flagged: by the letter's numbers, Anthropic is paying SpaceX about 60% more for the same compute than in May, on mostly older Hopper chips, with a 90-day exit clause. @firesidealpha's notes put the lease at roughly 325,000 GPUs for $1.25 billion a month. When buyers pay more for old hardware they could walk away from, ren argues, the owners of compute hold the pricing power.
items.short: Anthropic is reportedly paying SpaceX about 60% more for the same older GPUs than in May.

items.headline: Chris Camillo: the public AI story and the private one have never been further apart
items.summary: "Never have I seen such a disconnect between the public narrative around AI and what I'm hearing privately," @ChrisCamillo wrote. Fear of collapse dominates X and the media, he said, while every business leader he talks to who is building and deploying AI says demand has never been stronger. In a follow-up he said he can't think of any AI news that would shift investor sentiment for good right now, because the bearish spin gets more attention.
items.short: Chris Camillo says builders report record AI demand while the public mood expects a collapse.

items.author: David Senra
items.text:
Vlad was a UCLA grad student making $18,000 a year when he decided to leave and start a company. 

Before he took this leap of faith he asked the vice chair of the department for a leave of absence. His advice changed the trajectory of Vlad’s life:

“I was biting my fingernails off for this conversation. I still remember it vividly. If he told me he wouldn’t approve the leave of absence I would have stayed back and kept doing grad school.”

I go into his office and he said, in a thick Russian accent: 

“So you want to be businessman? When I was your age, I also wanted business. I wish you could luck. You do it and we will have spot for you if it doesn’t work out.” 

“He gave me the safety net I needed to make the jump.”

items.author: Serenity
items.text:
In terms of laser industry dynamics: 

- $LITE: "Take or pay. There's a very strong commitment from the customer side, and in some cases, there's a prepay element as well". Hyperscalers were explicitly funding their capacity expansion as well

- $COHR: Upfront payments in almost every LTA, according to its CEO. 

Both Lumentum and Coherent are the gold standard in terms of financing + demand signals. 

- For Chinese laser suppliers:

Optical module makers are actively financing their supply chains (even for lower range pluggables), as seen with Cambridge. 

In terms of US supply chains: 

- $AAOI CFO gave a note: "Customer financing is more likely for emerging technologies such as CPO and NPO than conventional 800G and 1.6T transceivers."

- $AAOI got a CPO + laser contract worth $700m for 2028-2029. But resulted in more ATMs instead of funding expansion with prepayments... 

I think people can agree AOI as a business at $3.7B MC is very operationally compelling:

- since they signed a $1B-$1.5B LTA with one hyperscaler
-  $2.2B LTA all in a single quarter.

But with management repeatedly creates expectations that later disclosures contrast with, which I agree is strange. 

Lot of current financing (as seen with Neoclouds) are done with prepayments given tightening. Or if a supplier is important enough (as seen with $SPCX), they'll help refinance the company. 

So I'm really not sure what's happening with $AAOI, maybe it's overstated competitive positioning or something else. 

I still think $AAOI is looks compelling H2 2027, but their biggest problem is their own financing methods and management credibility not customer demand.

items.headline: Letter: neoclouds trade near the value of capacity they've already signed
items.summary: Per @ren_stocks' reading of the Situational Awareness letter, CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN trade at roughly 1.0 to 1.2 times the value of their live and signed capacity, giving no credit for power secured but not yet sold. Nebius is targeting 0.8 to 1 GW connected against 4+ GW contracted, and signed its Q3 deals above $25 million per MW a year, up from $20-25 million in Q2.

items.headline: Micron's CHIPS Act buyback limits start lifting Dec. 9
items.summary: @aleabitoreddit notes Dec. 9 ends the first two years under Micron's initial CHIPS Act agreements, which restricted buybacks; Micron has said it expects to return 100% of excess cash to shareholders and raise returns after that date. SK Hynix doubled its daily buybacks after Korea relaxed its rules. TrendForce expects conventional DRAM contract prices up 10-15% in Q4 and 3-8% in Q1 2027.

items.headline: NAND spot prices keep falling
items.summary: @VJNCapital points out that NAND prices continue to slide, with DDR4 8Gb spot down 7% since October. NAND makes up all of SanDisk's revenue and about a quarter of Samsung's, SK Hynix's and Micron's, and he argues the memory selloff won't stop until spot prices stabilize.

items.title: Four Cards
items.rule: If a parcel is marked Express, it has a red sticker.
items.explanation: Express could hide something that breaks the rule; No sticker breaks it if the other side turns out to be Express. Red sticker can't break it (the rule never says only those cards have it), and Standard isn't covered by the rule at all. Most people pick the card that matches the rule's second half instead of the one that could falsify it.
